paras: The Pueblo lynchings of March 1882 were the hanging of five men accused of cattle stealing by a masked band in and near Pueblo, Colorado, on the night of March 30-31, 1882. The band took W. T. Phebus and Jay W. McGrew from the Pueblo county jail and hanged them on Santa Fe avenue, then rode to a ranch about ten miles away and hanged two Chastine brothers and Frank Owsby. The case drew notice for its scale, five men in one night, and for a damages suit against Pueblo county over prisoners taken from its custody.

Phebus and McGrew were held in the Pueblo county jail on a charge of cattle stealing, and another prisoner, Sanderson, was held there on the same charge. A Pueblo dispatch described a county Cattle Growers Association, a branch of the state body formed by cattle growers for the protection of their property.

Early in the morning a party of sixteen masked men gained admittance to the jail by claiming to be deputy sheriffs bringing in a prisoner, and they bound and gagged the jailer, named in one report as Strait. They took Phebus and McGrew out and hanged them to a tree on Santa Fe avenue, within 100 yards of the jail. The first wire said it was done so quietly that it was not known until late morning.

The band then rode about ten miles from Pueblo to a ranch, given as Reynolds' place on the St. Charles road or as Chastine's ranch, and surrounded the house. There they captured S. P. Chastine, his brother, called Billy, Berry or Barry, and Frank Owsby, bound their hands, took them on horseback to a patch of timber and hanged them. One digest said the men waited to be sure their victims were dead, and the Daily Republican said they were all in their beds by morning.

No report of an inquest or arrests appears in the coverage, and the Daily Republican said no trace could be found of any man who had been away from home. The lynchers were not identified, though the wires said they were believed to be members of the Cattle Growers' Protective Association. Phebus's widow went to Pueblo to claim his remains and told the Denver Times that the Foremans, brothers-in-law of Sanderson, had procured the lynching, asking why the cattle growers had left Sanderson in jail.

The Denver Times reported that Mrs. Phebus was suing Pueblo county for $5,000 because her husband was lynched while in the custody of county officials. A Pueblo dispatch of April 7 said friends of the men would sue for $50,000, and in May papers reported that the families had filed such a suit; no outcome appears in the coverage.

White papers across the country carried the story within days, most in short wire items that called the victims 'cattle thieves' or 'notorious cattle thieves' without qualification. The Cheyenne Daily Leader headed the first wire 'Speedy Justice' and the next day called the five 'well-known cattle thieves', while the Daily Republican headed its account 'A Quiet Lyric Party'. A weekly news digest reprinted in Tennessee called Phebus and McGrew 'eminent horse-thieves' and said a 'necktie' was ready for the last of the gang.

Distant reprints often garbled the place, setting the lynching in Denver or in 'Pueblo, New Mexico', and the names, which appear as Plebus, McGraw, McGren and McGrou. Some western voices were critical: the Denver Times called it 'mob violence' and suggested that county liability might make officials protect prisoners. A month later the Barbour County Index in Kansas said McGrew, a former resident of Sun City township, had been 'esteemed for his integrity' and called his death a murder 'without a shadow of justification'. An address on a Seattle lynching listed Pueblo among recent cases of lynch law, and no report states the race of any of the five men.

The earliest Pueblo wire put the jail lynching a little after midnight, while specials dated April 1 gave between 2 and 3 a.m. 'this morning'. Most reports gave the band as sixteen men, but the Denver Tribune's special said it grew from twelve to twenty-five before the ranch hangings.

reader.title: Pueblo lynchings of March 1882
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Masked men took two prisoners held on a cattle-theft charge from the Pueblo county jail and hanged them, then hanged three more men at a ranch (A4, A6, A9).

A band of about sixteen men with no lawful authority overpowered the jailer, took Phebus and McGrew from jail and hanged them, then hanged three others, all as accused cattle thieves (A6, A9, A17). The victims' race is never stated, so whether this is anti-Black violence is a scope question, not a verdict question.

Separate Pueblo wires (Associated Press via Cheyenne and New York, the Times special, the Tribune special) and a Denver Times follow-up agree on the jail lynching and the ranch hangings (A1, A4, A6, A9, A16).
